title: Scooby-Doo
full_review:
Zoinks! The Mystery Inc. gang reunites to solve the baffling events taking place at Spooky Island in the intermittently amusing comedy "Scooby-Doo" (Warner Bros.).

"Scooby-Doo" can often be entertaining in a silly way as it remains true to its cartoon roots while poking fun at the characters' distinctive trademark features. In fact, the funniest moments come when the film acknowledges what Scooby-Doo fans may have been thinking all along about Fred's narcissism, Daphne's vanity and inability to defend herself, Velma's contempt for Fred and just what exactly is in those Scooby snacks. And the comedy has all the hallmarks of a classic Scooby-Doo mystery: a haunted amusement park, a villain in disguise and, most importantly, a bunch of meddling kids.

However, parents may be dismayed at the film's unnecessary inclusion of cleavage-revealing outfits, rude humor and innuendos that vaguely reference pot smoking and sexuality. Most, if not all, of these jokes will go over the heads of youngsters, so it seems foolish to even include them. However, what is more troublesome is that this PG-rated film is aimed at a younger audience who doesn't need to be exposed to this material no matter how mild it is (and for the most part it is pretty mild).

All the groovy crime-solving cohorts from the Hanna-Barbera animated TV series are well and accounted for. The confident leader of the Mystery Inc. is ascot-wearing Fred (Freddie Prinze Jr.), who inevitably takes credit for all the work. The real brains behind the outfit is Velma (Linda Cardellini), who, hidden behind her thick, black-framed glasses and bulky tangerine sweater, is usually eclipsed by her mystery-solving companions.

Redheaded fashion plate Daphne (Sarah Michelle Gellar) is the damsel in distress who inevitably finds herself whisked away by the bad guys. Rounding out the crew is gangly Shaggy (Matthew Lillard), Scooby's best buddy, whose constant junk-food cravings are matched by Great Dane Scooby's (voiced by Neil Fanning) insatiable hunger for Scooby snacks. Both Shaggy and Scooby are a matched set, ready to run away from any and all danger while the rest of the team looks for clues.

Also similar to the TV series, the film's skimpy, and sometimes confusing, story follows a formulaic path from setup to final discovery of who's behind the caper. Two years after the Mystery Inc. gang has gone their separate ways because of jealousies and resentments (which allows director Raja Gosnell to inject a bit of good-natured satire into the film by poking fun at each of the characters' vanity spots), the team is reunited at Spooky Island, a haunted house theme park that is a popular spring break spot for college coeds.

Each has been invited by the resort's owner, Emile Mondavarious (Rowan Atkinson), who claims that strange things have been happening on the island. It seems that some supernatural forces have been transforming the normally upbeat coeds into sober, straight-laced students (a problem the Ft. Lauderdale police would surely love to have during spring break each year).

The Mystery Inc. members suspect an actual person behind this supposed paranormal activity, which somehow includes an ambiguous ancient ritual that steals away the teens' spirits. The scary scenes in the film are very similar to the sort of violence seen in cartoons: lots of running and bumbling about without anyone really being hurt. The film's computer-generated effects are top-notch. Live action is seamlessly blended with the animation as actors convincingly interact with the computer-generated Scooby, whose lively facial expressions and movements are both funny and fun to watch.

Although all the actors deviate very little in their performances from their animated alter egos, Lillard stands out as the scrawny Shaggy. Mimicking the voice, slouch, and awkward movements, Lillard brings Shaggy to life, as if he leapt off the animated page onto the screen.

Among the tongue-in-cheek humor, "Scooby-Doo" throws in a slight lesson on the value of teamwork as the Mystery Inc. gang finds that they are best when they work together. And cameos by rock band Sugar Ray and Pamela Anderson bring the film screaming into the 21st century.

Due to some scary action sequences and puerile humor, and a few crass expressions and innuendos, the U.S. Conference of Catholic Bishops classification is A-II- adults and adolescents. The Motion Picture Association of America rating is PG- parental guidance suggested.
(
2002
)
